newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Rolls-Royce fans bullish on Hong Kong outlook.
newsitem.headline: Rolls-Royce fans bullish on Hong Kong outlook.

text.p: Business is booming for Rolls-Royce Plc in Hong Kong, a sure sign this wealthy community's super-rich are optimistic about the future after China takes control from Britain at midnight June 30.

"We sold 38 units (vehicles) in 1995 and 38 in 1996 but we have delivered 30 units already this year and have another 20 orders," Spenser Lam, manager of sales and marketing for Hong Kong's MD Motors, said on Wednesday.
"The year is not even half over and already we are about 40 per cent ahead of our Rolls-Royce sales for last year. This indicates that our customers are confident about Hong Kong and the future."

Public opinion poll results released on Tuesday indicated that 60 per cent of those surveyed in Hong Kong were "optimistic" about the post-handover period but many also harboured serious concerns about future corruption and restrictions on political freedoms.
Lam, whose company is the only Rolls-Royce dealer in Hong Kong, said there are 1,600 of the luxury automobiles in the territory, the highest number per capita anywhere in the world.

The Hong Kong Tourist Association reckons that one per cent of all the Rolls-Royces ever made can be found in Hong Kong. The Peninsula Hotel alone has a fleet of nine, including a vintage Silver Dawn model.

Basic models range in price from HK$ 3 million to HK$ 5.5 million (US$ 384,600 to US$ 705,128) including a 60 per cent sales tax. Custom orders take four months to build and another month for delivery.
MD Motors has sold about 70 Rolls Royces to customers from China since 1991.
"Our customers are special people. Sometimes they send their driver or secretary over for the brochure, sometimes they come in person," Lam said.

"We've had celebrities come into the showroom with big cigars and several assistants trailing them. We had a man come in with a suitcase full of cash and drive a car home off the showroom floor. Other customers have taken more than a year to make up their minds."
Lam has had his share of offbeat orders including Rolls-Royces with pink interiors and a few with what he called "the mafia look" -- full body armour and tinted, bullet-proof glass with curtains.
One couple even boasts his-and-hers Rolls-Royces - a pink Silver Shadow and a sparkling Gold Phantom.

The basic Rolls-Royce comes with leather seats and air conditioning but Hong Kong customers like to add the "entertainment" package of laser-disc, compact disc, television and arm-rest bottle cooler. Faxes and computers are popular options but car phones are not.
"Everyone in Hong Kong has a cellular telephone and our customers prefer to use them because they can carry them everywhere," Lam said.

MD Motors also offers Bentleys, which Lam describes as better suited for "customers who want the self-driving experience" rather than a chauffered existence in what reports say is the world's densest traffic.

The Mercedes Benz is also a wildly popular automobile here. By one account there are more than 30,000 Mercedes in Hong Kong -- about 11.6 per cent of all the private cars in the territory and a higher market share than Mercedes has in Germany, where they are made.
Hong Kong has one of the lowest ratios of private car ownership in the world but the automotive fetish among its wealthy is sometimes carried to absurd lengths.

A single-digit vanity licence plate was auctioned off at a government charity fund raiser in 1994 for the princely sum of HK$13 million (US$1.7 million). The digit was "nine", which in the Cantonese dialect widely spoken in Hong Kong sounds like the word for longevity.
